summary: This entry describes the Fe-35Mn-17Al-5Cu (at.%) low-density steel designated "17Al" in the aged state obtained by solution treatment at 1100 °C for 10 min (oil quench) followed by aging at 625 °C for 10 h and water quenching. The sample belongs to a study of how Al content controls the aging-hardening behaviour of Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels. At 625 °C the α (BCC) matrix has essentially fully transformed to an ultra-hard β-Mn matrix that hosts fine new BCC and FCC Cu-rich precipitates, giving a Vickers hardness of 870.5 ± 24.9 HV against an as-solutionised baseline of 259.8 ± 1.5 HV.
composition: Nominal composition Fe-35Mn-17Al-5Cu (at.%). EDS-measured chemistry (Table 1): Fe 43.2, Mn 34.8, Al 17.0, Cu 5.0 at.%. Across the 15Al/17Al/19Al series the Mn (~35 at.%) and Cu (~5 at.%) levels are held essentially constant while the rising Al is accommodated by substituting for Fe, so 17Al sits between 15Al (15.0 Al, 44.6 Fe) and 19Al (18.6 Al, 41.6 Fe). Design intent: Mn at a high 35 at.% promotes the precipitation kinetics of the hard β-Mn phase; Al is the primary density-reducing element (~0.1 g/cm³ per 1 wt.% Al) and also governs β-Mn precipitation and the Al-rich D0₃ phase; Cu is added to accelerate the aging-hardening response and raise the hardness of the Fe-Mn-Al-Cu steel. The measured density of the 17Al alloy is 6.76 g/cm³.
processing: Production sequence: (1) vacuum induction melting of high-purity (>99.9 %) raw materials under an argon atmosphere to give the Fe-35Mn-17Al-5Cu ingot; (2) homogenization at 1200 °C for 24 h; (3) hot rolling into plates 4 mm thick; (4) electrical discharge machining into 10 × 5 × 2 mm³ specimens for hardness and microstructure work; (5) solution treatment at 1100 °C for 10 min under argon followed by oil quenching, which yields a single-phase α (BCC) matrix with a baseline hardness of 259.8 ± 1.5 HV. The defining step of this sample (state "625 °C–10 h") is (6) aging at 625 °C for 10 h followed by water quenching. The overall processing philosophy is a soft solution-treated state that is hardened afterwards by a short aging treatment.
microstructure: After high-temperature aging (600 °C and above) the α matrix of the 17Al alloy had almost completely transformed into β-Mn within just 1 h, so the 625 °C/10 h state consists essentially of a near-equiaxed β-Mn matrix (complex cubic) containing fine new BCC precipitates within the β-Mn and fine FCC Cu-rich particles at the β-Mn interfaces. Three phases are therefore present: β-Mn (dominant matrix), a new BCC phase, and an FCC Cu-rich phase. The FCC Cu-rich particles frequently contain FCC twins; the new BCC precipitates are of a size comparable to the FCC Cu-rich particles and sit within the β-Mn and at β-Mn interfaces. EBSD of 17Al shows an essentially uniform β-Mn field (e.g. at 575 °C/6 h and 650 °C/10 h) with the new FCC phase resolved at 575 °C/6 h and the new BCC phase at 650 °C/10 h. For 17Al the α→β-Mn transformation is complete after 6 h at 550 °C but after only 1 h at 600 °C and above. The FCC phase is rich in Cu, depleted in Fe and Mn and slightly poor in Al, whereas β-Mn is poor in Cu. The β-Mn in the hardest 17Al sample contains 36.2 at.% Mn, 16.3 at.% Al and 2.6 at.% Cu (measured on the 575 °C/6 h state). The phase-evolution sequence is α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase.
properties: Mechanical: Vickers hardness of this aged state (625 °C, 10 h) = 870.5 ± 24.9 HV, measured with a 9.8 N load for 15 s (five measurements averaged) on 10 × 5 × 2 mm³ specimens; the as-solutionised 17Al baseline is 259.8 ± 1.5 HV. Over the whole 17Al aging matrix the hardness spanned 259.8–924.9 HV, with the 625 °C and 650 °C series plateauing at roughly 813–878 HV. Physical: density 6.76 g/cm³ (Archimedes). The related peak-hardness 17Al state (575 °C/6 h, 924.9 HV) has a nanoindentation hardness of 11.1 ± 0.6 GPa and an intrinsic β-Mn hardness of 12.2 ± 0.1 GPa, and a fracture toughness K_IC of 6.6 MPa·m^1/2 (indentation method). No tensile properties (yield strength, UTS, elongation), fatigue, or creep data are reported. Characterization techniques applied to the aged 17Al alloy: X-ray diffraction (D8 Discover, 2θ 20–110°), secondary-electron SEM (ZEISS Sigma 300, 5 kV), EBSD (GeminiSEM 300; 1.5 μm low-magnification and 0.05 μm high-magnification step), TEM/HRTEM/SAED with EDS (FEI Talos F200X, 200 kV), nanoindentation (Agilent G200, 200 nm depth), and Vickers hardness testing (HVS-1000).
mechanisms: Complete α→β-Mn transformation is the origin of ultra-hardening: aging the 17Al alloy at 625 °C (≥600 °C) fully converts the BCC α matrix into β-Mn within just 1 h, and because β-Mn has a very high intrinsic hardness (~12.2 GPa measured by nanoindentation for 17Al) the alloy reaches a plateau hardness around 870 HV; the ultra-high hardness is thus governed by the volume fraction of β-Mn rather than by any single precipitating phase.

β-Mn precipitation is diffusion-controlled: β-Mn is an Mn-rich phase whose nucleation and growth require long-range diffusion that enriches Mn while rejecting large amounts of Fe, Al and Cu into the surrounding matrix, so the transformation is accelerated at higher aging temperatures by an enhanced driving force and faster atomic diffusion.

Increasing Al content slows β-Mn precipitation kinetics: more Al must be expelled around the growing β-Mn and a greater amount of the Al-rich D0₃ phase is stabilized after solution treatment, so β-Mn nucleation/growth (which requires depletion of D0₃) is retarded — the 17Al alloy therefore transforms more slowly than 15Al and needs longer or hotter aging to complete the α→β-Mn reaction.

BCC precipitate formation at β-Mn interfaces: because β-Mn expels Al into the surrounding matrix, the interfaces between β-Mn become enriched in the BCC-stabilizing element Al, inducing precipitation of the fine new BCC phase between the β-Mn.

Cu-rich FCC precipitate formation: the limited solubility of Cu in Fe-based alloys, combined with the expulsion of Cu from β-Mn during its precipitation and growth, produces the fine FCC Cu-rich particles at the β-Mn interfaces, which frequently contain FCC twins.

Al-driven hardness–toughness trade-off: raising Al slightly increases the intrinsic hardness of β-Mn by solid-solution strengthening (Al in β-Mn rises from 14.3 at.% in 15Al to 16.3 at.% in 17Al), but also increases the fraction of softer BCC and FCC Cu-rich interphases and decreases the ductile Cu-rich phase, lowering both the overall micro-hardness and the fracture toughness of the ultra-hard alloys (K_IC 6.6 MPa·m^1/2 for 17Al vs 8.6 MPa·m^1/2 for 15Al).
conclusions: This 625 °C/10 h state illustrates the design logic of the Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steel: a simple aging treatment converts a soft single-phase α (BCC) matrix (259.8 HV) into an ultra-hard β-Mn matrix (~870 HV) through continuous β-Mn precipitation, so the hardness is tunable simply by aging temperature and time. Within the alloy series, increasing Al content (15→17→19 at.%) slows β-Mn precipitation kinetics and lowers both the final hardening effect and the fracture toughness; consequently the hardness of 17Al at 625 °C/10 h (870.5 HV) lies below the 15Al peak of 965.6 HV, and 17Al's own peak (924.9 HV) is reached at 575 °C/6 h. The alloy family achieves an ultrawide tunable hardness window (253.4–965.6 HV) and a maximum specific hardness above 140 HV·cm³/g, supporting a "one type of material, multiple uses" concept for lightweight structural parts formed in the soft state and then aged. The remaining limitation is that the toughness of the ultra-hard states (e.g. K_IC 6.6 MPa·m^1/2 for the hardest 17Al sample) is still not good enough, so optimising the hardness–toughness balance warrants further study.
unmapped: The β-Mn composition reported for the 17Al alloy (36.2 at.% Mn, 16.3 at.% Al, 2.6 at.% Cu) was measured on the hardest sample (575 °C/6 h), not on the 625 °C/10 h state; a composition specific to the 625 °C/10 h state is not given.

No tensile/elongation, fracture-toughness or specific-hardness value is reported specifically for the 625 °C/10 h condition; the quoted K_IC (6.6 MPa·m^1/2) and specific-hardness figures pertain to the series' hardest states.
